# The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law

A completed local closure can return exactly to its starting state.

Its native multiplicity can also close exactly:

$$
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0.
$$

But this does not require the two opposed directions around the closure to be
realized with equal occurrence-count efficiency.

R<sup>2</sup>D identifies this distinction as the primitive origin of
irreversibility.

> **Structural closure can be exact while occurrence realization is
> nonreciprocal.**

The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law then makes an additional cross-boundary
statement:

> **Local occurrence-count nonreciprocity is read at the enclosing boundary
> as an increment in nondirectional background.**

Formally,

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
\geq0.
}
$$

This is the Second Law of Recursive Counting.

## Closure Does Not Require Reversibility

Consider a completed local closure

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}:
i
\rightarrow
k
\rightarrow
i.
$$

The state has returned.

Therefore its native multiplicity closes:

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0.
}
$$

But there is another question:

> **Were the two opposed legs realized equally often?**

The answer need not be yes.

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D separates **closure** from **reversibility**.

[Closure →](closure.qmd)

## Directional Occurrence-Count Efficiency

Let

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
$$

be the realized occurrence count of one oriented leg of the closure.

Let

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
$$

be the occurrence count of the opposed return leg.

Define the directional occurrence-count efficiency

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}.
}
$$

Choose the orientation such that

$$
0<
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
\leq1.
$$

If the two opposed directions are realized equally,

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
=
\nu_{n,\alpha,H},
$$

then

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=1.
}
$$

The closure is occurrence-count reciprocal.

## Nonreciprocal Realization

If

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
<
\nu_{n,\alpha,H},
$$

then

$$
\boxed{
0<
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
<1.
}
$$

The structural cycle still closes.

But its two opposed directions are not realized with equal count efficiency.

This is the primitive R<sup>2</sup>D definition of irreversible realization.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{irreversibility}
\neq
\text{failure of state closure}.
}
$$

Instead,

$$
\boxed{
\text{irreversibility}
=
\text{nonreciprocal occurrence realization around closure}.
}
$$

## Occurrence-Count Loss

R<sup>2</sup>D represents this directional inefficiency logarithmically.

Define

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}
\right).
}
$$

Because

$$
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
},
$$

we can also write

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
-\ln
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
$$

For reciprocal realization,

$$
\eta=1,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
L_\tau=0.
}
$$

For nonreciprocal realization,

$$
0<\eta<1,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
L_\tau>0.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
L_\tau\geq0.
}
$$

## "Loss" Does Not Mean Destruction

The word **loss** requires care.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not propose that occurrence count is annihilated.

Nor does it propose that multiplicity is destroyed.

Nor does it propose that direction disappears.

The quantity

$$
L_\tau
$$

measures a **logarithmic deficit in reciprocal directional realization**.

It says that one opposed leg is realized less efficiently than the other.

Thus:

> **Occurrence-count loss is nonreciprocity, not count destruction.**

## Exact Multiplicity Closure Can Coexist With Irreversibility

This gives one of the cleanest relations in Part I:

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
}
$$

while simultaneously

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}>0.
}
$$

The first statement says:

> native possible multiplicity closes exactly.

The second says:

> realized occurrence count is directionally nonreciprocal.

These are different count relations.

So an irreversible closure does not require a failure of the underlying
multiplicity structure to close.

## Possible Count and Realized Count Behave Differently

This distinction returns us to the separation between multiplicity and
occurrence.

Multiplicity is possible count:

$$
W.
$$

Occurrence is realized count:

$$
\nu.
$$

The closure condition

$$
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0
$$

belongs to possible count.

The irreversible condition

$$
L_\tau>0
$$

belongs to realized occurrence count.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{possible-count closure}
\neq
\text{occurrence-count reciprocity}.
}
$$

[Occupancy and Occurrence →](occupancy-occurrence.qmd)

## Background Is a Different Kind of Count

R<sup>2</sup>D now introduces **background**.

Let a local peer boundary \(\alpha\) have a positive background count

$$
b_{n,\alpha}>0.
$$

Define its logarithmic coordinate

$$
\boxed{
\Phi_{n,\alpha}
=
\ln b_{n,\alpha}.
}
$$

Background is not another local directional state.

Within peer boundary \(\alpha\), it is common to the local macrostates.

Thus, for a local transition

$$
i\rightarrow k,
$$

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\Phi_{n,\alpha,i\rightarrow k}=0.
}
$$

Background therefore does not independently favor one local macrostate over
another.

## Background Is Nondirectional Locally

This gives background its defining local property.

At the boundary where it is background,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\Phi=0.
}
$$

It does not supply a local directional tilt.

So background is fundamentally different from

$$
\Delta P,
$$

$$
\Delta R,
$$

or

$$
\Delta A.
$$

Those quantities distinguish directions within the local state domain.

Background does not.

> **Background is nondirectional relative to the boundary at which it is
> background.**

## But Background Is Boundary Relative

Now consider two peer boundaries,

$$
\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\beta.
$$

Their local background coordinates might be

$$
\Phi_{n,\alpha}
$$

and

$$
\Phi_{n,\beta}.
$$

Each is nondirectional within its own peer boundary.

But the enclosing boundary can compare them.

Define

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\Phi_{n+1|n,\alpha:\beta}
=
\Phi_{n,\alpha}
-
\Phi_{n,\beta}.
}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\Phi_{n+1|n,\alpha:\beta}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
b_{n,\alpha}
}{
b_{n,\beta}
}
\right).
}
$$

If this quantity is nonzero, then the enclosing boundary can distinguish a
relation between the two subordinate backgrounds.

So:

> **What is nondirectional background at one boundary can become part of a
> distinguishable relation at an enclosing boundary.**

Background is therefore boundary relative, just like state identity itself.

## The Enclosing Background Increment

Now consider one completed representative local closure.

Let

$$
b_{n+1}^{-}
$$

denote the enclosing background count before the associated realization,

and

$$
b_{n+1}^{+}
$$

the enclosing background count afterward.

Define the logarithmic background increment

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
b_{n+1}^{+}
}{
b_{n+1}^{-}
}
\right).
}
$$

This is an enclosing-boundary count relation.

It is not the same object as the local occurrence-count loss.

The Second Law relates the two.

## The Second-Law Postulate

R<sup>2</sup>D postulates that the local logarithmic occurrence-count loss and
the enclosing logarithmic background increment are two boundary-specific
readings of one recursively organized realization.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
}
$$

Substituting the occurrence counts,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}
\right).
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
\geq0.
}
$$

## Reciprocal Realization Produces No Background Increment

If

$$
\eta=1,
$$

then

$$
L_\tau=0.
$$

The Second Law gives

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}=0.
}
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\eta=1
\iff
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}=0.
}
$$

Reciprocal local realization corresponds to no Second-Law background
increment.

## Nonreciprocal Realization Produces a Positive Background Increment

If

$$
0<\eta<1,
$$

then

$$
L_\tau>0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}>0.
}
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
0<\eta<1
\iff
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}>0.
}
$$

The primitive irreversible relation is therefore nonnegative.

## This Is Not Bottom-Up Transfer

The equation

$$
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
$$

must not be read as

$$
\text{lost local count}
\longrightarrow
\text{background substance}.
$$

No destroyed count is physically transported upward.

The local quantity and enclosing quantity are defined at different
boundaries.

They are two boundary-specific readings.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{local nonreciprocity}
\longleftrightarrow
\text{enclosing background increment}.
}
$$

The equality is between logarithmic count coordinates.

It is not arithmetic equality between raw counts.

## The Causal Direction Does Not Reverse

The Second Law also does not reverse the causal inversion developed earlier.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not say that local occurrence-count loss **causes** the
enclosing background.

The enclosing-to-local causal architecture remains

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
}
$$

The Second Law says how one realized relation is read differently at the two
boundaries.

As with recursive carry, cross-boundary correspondence must not be confused
with upward causation.

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Productive Output Does Not Define Irreversibility

The enclosing constraint can be decomposed as

$$
C_{n+1}
=
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
+
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}.
$$

The productive component is associated with retained distinguishable output:

$$
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}
\lambda_{n+1}.
$$

The background-associated component is associated with realization read as
background:

$$
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}
\lambda_{n+1}.
$$

But productive output does not determine whether a closure is irreversible.

The irreversibility criterion remains

$$
\boxed{
L_\tau>0.
}
$$

For example,

$$
C_{n+1}^{\mathrm{out}}=0
$$

does not imply

$$
L_\tau=0.
$$

A system can retain no productive distinguishable output and still realize
its opposed closure legs nonreciprocally.

## Zero Productive Output Is Not Reversibility

This distinction is important physically.

A process can produce no useful output and still be irreversible.

Likewise, productive output can be present without itself defining the
degree of irreversibility.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{productive output}
\neq
\text{irreversibility}.
}
$$

Irreversibility is determined by the reciprocity of occurrence realization
around closure.

## The Background-Associated Constraint Is Not the Background Increment

Two quantities must remain distinct:

$$
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}\lambda_{n+1}
$$

and

$$
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}.
$$

The first belongs to the decomposition of the total constrained enclosing
realization.

The second belongs to the Second-Law correspondence with local occurrence
nonreciprocity.

Part I does **not** postulate

$$
C_{n+1}^{\Phi}\lambda_{n+1}
=
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}.
$$

A later physical mapping may relate their physical reads in a particular
system.

That is a separate empirical question.

## The R<sup>2</sup>D Law and Second Law Do Different Jobs

The R<sup>2</sup>D law is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
C_{n+1}
\lambda_{n+1}
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}.
}
$$

It relates:

> **local recurrence-weighted asymmetry**

to

> **enclosing recurrence-weighted constrained distinguishability.**

The Second Law is

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}.
}
$$

It relates:

> **local occurrence-count nonreciprocity**

to

> **enclosing nondirectional background increment.**

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{R²D law}
\neq
\text{R²D Second Law}.
}
$$

They are complementary postulates.

[The R²D Law →](r2d-law.qmd)

## Asymmetry Is Not Irreversibility

Another distinction follows.

Closure asymmetry is

$$
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
-
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
$$

Occurrence nonreciprocity is measured by

$$
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
$$

These are not the same relation.

A closure can be asymmetrically organized while its opposed occurrence counts
remain reciprocal.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}\neq0
\not\Rightarrow
L_\tau>0.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore separates:

> **directionality**

from

> **irreversibility**.

Direction tells us which realization is favored.

Irreversibility tells us whether opposed realization occurs with equal
directional efficiency.

## Closure, Direction, and Irreversibility Are Three Different Questions

For one completed cycle, ask:

### Did the state return?

For a closure, yes.

### Is the enclosing relation directional?

Possibly:

$$
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}\neq0.
$$

### Are the opposed realization counts reciprocal?

Possibly not:

$$
L_\tau>0.
$$

These questions are independent enough that they require separate
mathematical quantities.

This is one of the reasons R<sup>2</sup>D does not identify irreversibility
simply with "the system moved downhill."

## Nothing Is Destroyed

The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law can therefore be stated without invoking
destruction.

Native multiplicity closes:

$$
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0.
$$

The local state closes.

Occurrence continues.

Direction can remain.

What fails to be reciprocal is the **efficiency with which opposed
directions realize occurrence count**.

The logarithmic difference is

$$
L_\tau.
$$

At the enclosing boundary, that same recursive relation is read as

$$
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi.
$$

Thus:

> **Nothing must disappear for irreversibility to exist.**

The primitive irreversible relation is a change in **how count is realized
and subsequently classified across boundaries**.

## Why This Resembles the Thermodynamic Second Law

The structure is deliberately suggestive.

Thermodynamic irreversibility is associated with nonnegative entropy
production.

R<sup>2</sup>D has now produced a primitive nonnegative count relation:

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
\geq0.
}
$$

But Part I has not yet identified

$$
\Phi
$$

with thermodynamic entropy.

It has not yet introduced temperature or heat.

The thermodynamic Second Law is therefore not assumed here.

Instead, Part II asks whether thermodynamic entropy production is a physical
read of this more primitive recursive-count relation.

[From Count to Physical Science →](from-count-to-physics.qmd)

## The Empirical Burden

The Second Law of Recursive Counting is a postulate.

The definitions of

$$
\eta
$$

and

$$
L_\tau
$$

follow from occurrence counts.

The statement

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
}
$$

is an additional R<sup>2</sup>D claim.

A physical realization must therefore establish independently:

- the relevant closure;
- its opposed occurrence counts;
- the resulting \(L_\tau\);
- the appropriate enclosing boundary;
- and the corresponding background increment.

Only then can the proposed correspondence be tested.

The later thermodynamic program carries that empirical burden.

## The Primitive Second-Law Architecture

The complete structure can be written:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{local closure}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\Delta S_{\mathcal C}=0
\\[8pt]
\text{opposed occurrence realization}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\eta_{\mathcal C}
=
\dfrac{\nu_L}{\nu_H}
\\[8pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
L_\tau
=
-\ln\eta_{\mathcal C}
\geq0
\\[8pt]
\Longleftrightarrow
\\[8pt]
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
\geq0
\\[4pt]
\text{enclosing background increment}
\end{array}
}
$$

The native structure closes.

The realized directional efficiencies need not.

The enclosing boundary reads the difference as background.

## Core Equations

### Native multiplicity closure

$$
\boxed{
\Delta S_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
}
$$

### Directional occurrence-count efficiency

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}
}
$$

### Reciprocal realization

$$
\boxed{
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=1
\iff
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}=0
}
$$

### Nonreciprocal realization

$$
\boxed{
0<
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
<1
\iff
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}>0
}
$$

### Occurrence-count loss

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
-\ln
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}
\right)
}
$$

### Background increment

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
b_{n+1}^{+}
}{
b_{n+1}^{-}
}
\right)
}
$$

### The Second Law of Recursive Counting

$$
\boxed{
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\delta_{\mathcal C}\Phi_{n+1}
\geq0
}
$$

---

## The Key Distinction

The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law does not say that entropy-like substance is
created because something has been destroyed.

It says:

> **A local structure can close exactly while its opposed realization counts
> are nonreciprocal.**

> **That logarithmic nonreciprocity is read from the enclosing boundary as
> nondirectional background.**

So the primitive second-law architecture is

$$
\boxed{
\text{exact structural closure}
+
\text{nonreciprocal realization}
\longleftrightarrow
\text{enclosing background increment}.
}
$$

This separates structural closure, directionality, irreversibility, and
background before thermodynamic entropy has been introduced.
